1121.title: Giving without resting on anything (section 4)
1121.hook: give without dwelling on the gift, and the merit is boundless as space
1121.howItsDone: In Mahayana practice, giving is the first of the perfections, and section 4 of the Diamond Sutra is studied as its deepest form: a gift given without resting on the object, the receiver or the giver.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all beings freed, and none freed: help every being, but keep no tally. Your line: no one to count.

A birthday present goes out in the mail. A few days later, the sender feels a small itch: did it arrive? Did they like it? Why haven't they said anything? The gift has left their hands, but part of them is still holding the string. The Diamond Sutra, in its fourth section, takes up giving, the first of the perfections, and asks what happens if you cut the string completely. Its answer reaches for the biggest picture it can find: the sky in every direction.
screen: `A PRESENT IN THE MAIL.` → `STILL HOLDING THE STRING.` → `CUT THE STRING.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. The Buddha tells Subhuti that a bodhisattva should give a gift without resting on anything. Not resting on the thing given. Not on sights, sounds, smells, tastes, things touched, or things thought. Give, and don't lean your weight on the gift, or on the idea of it, or on the picture of yourself giving it. Second, the question about space. Then the Buddha asks: Subhuti, is it easy to measure the space to the east? No, Subhuti says. And to the south, the west, the north, below, above, and every direction between? No, each time. The question repeats, direction after direction, until the listener is standing in the middle of an open sky. Third, the point. In the same way, the Buddha says, the merit of a bodhisattva who gives without resting on anything is not easy to measure. Yesterday the sutra said keep no count of beings. Today it says the merit of that kind of giving can't be counted either. Let go of the counting, and what's left is too large to count. Fourth, why space. Space doesn't keep anything. Sunlight, birds, a thrown ball pass through it, and it isn't any smaller afterward. A gift that rests on nothing is like that: it goes out and doesn't come back on a string. Some readers find this hard, because noticing a gift is human, and a thank-you is a kindness too. The sutra doesn't forbid the thank-you. It asks the giver not to wait for it.
screen: `GIVE, AND DON'T LEAN ON IT.` · `CAN YOU MEASURE THE SKY?` · `MERIT NOT EASY TO MEASURE.` · `SPACE KEEPS NOTHING.` · then, large: `BOUNDLESS AS SPACE.`

segments.voice: Choose something small you could give, a note, a compliment, your full attention for five minutes, and picture handing it over and opening your hand. Feel the hand empty, then let your attention drift out in every direction, east, west, north, south, above, below, as far as the sky goes. When the thought of the gift returns, let it pass through, like a bird.
Giving without resting on anything. A gift that leans on nothing, not the object, not the thanks, not the giver, and merit that, like space, can't be measured. Today's word.
screen: `GIVING WITHOUT RESTING ON ANYTHING — today's word`.

1122.title: Not seen by marks (section 5)
1122.hook: can the Tathagata be known by bodily marks? no; where there are marks there is illusion
1122.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities the Diamond Sutra is chanted, copied and studied, and a short passage like this one is often read slowly and talked over with a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving without resting on anything: give, and don't keep dwelling on the gift. Your line: boundless as space.

A bronze Buddha sits behind museum glass. A rounded swell on the crown of the head, long earlobes, hair in small tight curls, a calm face with eyes half closed. Some of those features echo a list Buddhist tradition keeps: the marks of a great being, signs said to appear on the body of a Buddha. So here's a fair question. If a Buddha has marks, is that how you recognize one? Section five of the Diamond Sutra asks exactly that, and the Buddha is the one asking.
screen: `A BRONZE BUDDHA BEHIND GLASS.` → `THE MARKS OF A GREAT BEING.` → `IS THAT HOW YOU KNOW ONE?`

segments.voice: First, the question. The Buddha asks Subhuti: can the Tathagata be seen by means of his bodily marks? Tathagata is the name the Buddha uses for himself in the sutras. It's a test, and Subhuti doesn't take the easy answer. Second, the answer. No, Subhuti says, because the marks the Tathagata spoke of are no marks. The marks are named, and in the same breath they're said not to be what they seem. This sutra will do that again and again. Third, the line the section turns on. The Buddha agrees, and goes further: wherever there are marks, there is illusion; when you see that marks are no marks, you see the Tathagata. That's a paraphrase; the sutra's own words are short and strange, and translators put them differently. The point isn't that the statue is a lie, or that the body didn't matter. The sutra doesn't ask anyone to throw the statue out. It asks what you think you're seeing when you look at it. Fourth, the marks of a day. A uniform, an accent, a car, a job title, a wheelchair, a tattoo: each gets sorted in half a second. The sorting is useful. It's also, this sutra says, where the illusion starts, because the person never fits inside the mark. And the first picture the Diamond Sutra cuts through is the picture of the Buddha himself.

Not seen by marks. The Buddha isn't known by the body's signs; where there are marks, the sutra says, there is illusion. Today's word.
Your line: beyond the marks. Even the Buddha isn't seen by them. See you tomorrow.

1123.title: The raft again (section 6)
1123.hook: even the teaching is to be let go of, like a raft, and how much more what isn't the teaching
1123.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools use the raft picture to say that the teachings are tools for awakening, to be used fully and not clung to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not seen by marks: wherever there are marks, there is illusion. Your line: beyond the marks.

Subhuti has a practical worry. He has just heard that a Buddha can't be seen by his marks. So he asks what anyone who has explained something subtle to a skeptical friend might ask: in some later age, when people hear words like these, will anyone actually trust them? The Buddha says yes, there will be such people. Then he reaches for a picture this path has met before, in the older discourses: a raft, built for a river, and the question of what to do with it once you're across.
screen: `WILL ANYONE TRUST THIS?` → `YES, SAYS THE BUDDHA.` → `A RAFT, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the worry answered. In a later time, the Buddha says, there will be people who keep the precepts, and when they hear even a single line of this teaching, a clear trust will arise in them. Their roots of goodness, the sutra says, weren't planted with one Buddha only, but with countless Buddhas. Second, how they hold it. They don't grab hold of teachings, and they don't grab hold of the denial of teachings either. Clutching the teaching is one ditch; clutching the idea that nothing matters is the other. Third, the raft. That's why, the Buddha says, his teaching is to be understood as a raft. Even teachings are to be let go of, and how much more what isn't teaching. Fourth, the raft before this one. In the Pali discourses, in a sutta called the Water Snake, a man facing a great flood binds grass, sticks and branches into a raft and paddles across. On the far shore he wonders whether to hoist it onto his head and carry it with him, out of gratitude. No, the Buddha says. Leave it on the bank and go on. The teaching is for crossing over, not for holding on to. The Diamond Sutra pushes that old raft one step further: even the teaching itself, even this sutra. Nobody throws the raft away in the middle of the river. You need it on the water. The letting go comes when it has done its work.
screen: `WILL ANYONE TRUST THIS?` · `NOT TEACHING, NOT ITS DENIAL.` · `EVEN THE TEACHING IS A RAFT.` · `DON'T CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD.` · then, large: `FOR CROSSING, NOT FOR HOLDING.`

segments.voice: Find one rule you've carried a long time, something that once got you across a hard stretch: never ask for help, always be early, keep the peace at any price. Thank it, the way you might pat a raft that kept you dry, and ask: am I still on the river, or carrying this on my head? You don't have to decide; just set it on the bank for this sit, and breathe beside it.
The raft again. The teaching is a raft for crossing; even it is let go of, and how much more what isn't the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: even the raft. A raft is for the river, not the road. Same time tomorrow.

1124.title: Nothing fixed (section 7)
1124.hook: has the Tathagata attained anything? there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening
1124.howItsDone: Teachers in Mahayana schools, Zen among them, use this section to point out that awakening is not a possession to be gained.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the raft again: the teaching is for crossing, not for carrying on your head. Your line: even the raft.

A test question, with a trap folded inside. The Buddha asks Subhuti two things. Has the Tathagata attained the highest, complete awakening? And has the Tathagata taught any teaching? Anyone in that room could answer on reflex: yes, and yes. That's the whole story, isn't it? A seeker sits under a tree, wakes up, and spends his life teaching what he found. But Subhuti has been listening to this sutra, and he answers more carefully than that.
screen: `TWO QUESTIONS.` → `THE REFLEX ANSWER: YES AND YES.` → `SUBHUTI ANSWERS MORE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In the sutra's Sanskrit, that awakening has a long, grand name: anuttara samyak sambodhi, awakening that's complete, with nothing above it. Second, Subhuti's answer. As I understand what the Buddha has taught, he says, there is no fixed thing called the highest awakening, and no fixed teaching that the Tathagata has taught. No fixed thing: that's the phrase to hold, lightly. Third, the reason. What the Tathagata has taught, Subhuti says, can't be grasped and can't be spoken. It isn't a thing, and it isn't a no-thing either. Then a short line closes the section: the wise and holy ones are all set apart by the unconditioned, by what isn't put together from parts. Fourth, what this is not saying. It isn't saying the Buddha never woke up, or taught nothing, or that the teaching is empty talk. The rest of the sutra is a teaching, after all, and Subhuti is learning from it. It's saying awakening isn't an object he picked up and put in his pocket, something with edges you could hand over. Waking up in the morning isn't something you keep in a drawer, either. The same goes for smaller certainties. I'm the responsible one. She never listens. This job is who I am. Each one is useful. Held as a fixed thing, each starts to harden. The sutra keeps the hand open, even around the highest thing it knows.

1125.title: Four lines (section 8)
1125.hook: teaching even four lines of this sutra is worth more than worlds full of treasure
1125.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities, short passages of the Diamond Sutra are copied, recited and shared, and teachers point to this section when explaining why passing a teaching on is counted as merit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing fixed: there's no fixed thing called the highest awakening. Your line: nothing fixed.

Treasure enough to fill a world. Then another world, and another, until a whole vast system of worlds is heaped with gold and silver and jewels. Someone gives every bit of it away. The Buddha asks Subhuti: would that giver's merit be great? Very great, Subhuti says. Of course. Then the Buddha sets something on the other side of the scale, small enough to fit on an index card.
screen: `WORLDS HEAPED WITH TREASURE.` → `ALL OF IT GIVEN AWAY.` → `SOMETHING ON THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the scale. On one side, a world system filled with treasure, all of it given away. Subhuti agrees that's great merit, and adds a twist in the sutra's usual way: it's great because merit, too, isn't a fixed thing. Second, the other side. If someone takes up even a verse of four lines from this sutra, keeps it, and explains it to others, the Buddha says, that merit is greater. Not the whole sutra. Four lines, kept and passed on. Third, the reason. All the Buddhas, and their highest awakening, the sutra says, come out of this teaching. Teaching is where Buddhas come from, so passing even a little of it on outweighs the treasure. Then, right away, the sutra cuts its own praise: what is called the Buddha's teaching is not the Buddha's teaching. Even what it just lifted up gets no place to settle. Fourth, which four lines? The sutra doesn't say. Some readers point to the short verses this sutra contains. Others say it means any four lines of it, so the smallest piece is enough. Either way, the measure isn't size. A verse said to one person at a kitchen table counts. And notice who does the work: not the one who reads silently and keeps it to themselves, but the one who keeps it and explains it to someone else. Four lines can be a text message, a sticky note on a mirror, or what you say to a friend at a bad moment, when you remember something that once helped you.

1126.title: No "I have attained" (section 9)
1126.hook: a stream-enterer does not think "I have entered the stream"; Subhuti rests in peace without that thought
1126.tomorrow: A mind that rests on nothing (section 10)
1126.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, people are encouraged to do good quietly and to dedicate the merit to others rather than claim it; teachers use this section to warn against pride in one's own progress.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four lines: even a short verse, kept and passed on, outweighs worlds of treasure. Your line: four lines.

At some dinner parties there's a guest who mentions, more than once, how little he cares about status. The more he says it, the less it sounds true. Section nine of the Diamond Sutra is about the quiet opposite of that guest. The Buddha walks Subhuti down the stages of the path, and at every step he asks the same thing: does someone who has reached this stage think, I have reached it? At the end, Subhuti answers for himself, and he's the one the Buddha has praised.
screen: `THE GUEST WHO SAYS HE'S HUMBLE.` → `THE SAME QUESTION AT EVERY STEP.` → `SUBHUTI ANSWERS FOR HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the stages. Early Buddhist teaching names them: the stream-enterer, who has entered the current that leads to awakening; the once-returner; the non-returner; and the arhat, the worthy one, fully freed. Second, the question. Does a stream-enterer think, I have entered the stream? No, Subhuti says, and the reason is the sutra's own kind of reason. A stream-enterer enters nothing: not sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or things of the mind. That's exactly why the name stream-enterer can be used. The same question comes at each stage, and the same answer. An arhat who thought, I am an arhat, would be holding on to a self, a person, a being, a life, the very things the path lets go of. Third, Subhuti on himself. The Buddha has praised him, he says, as one who dwells in peace, free of craving. But I don't think, I am an arhat free of craving. If I did, the Buddha wouldn't have said that Subhuti delights in peaceful dwelling. The peace and the thought can't sit in the same chair. Fourth, the credit line. The sutra isn't against reaching anything, or against doing good; it names every stage. What it drops is the credit line written afterward, the small voice that says, look what I did. You carry a neighbor's groceries, and a minute later the narrator arrives to sign it. The groceries were carried either way.
screen: `THE STAGES OF THE PATH.` · `NO STREAM WAS ENTERED.` · `SUBHUTI DOESN'T SAY IT EITHER.` · `GOOD, WITHOUT THE CREDIT LINE.` · then, large: `NO "I HAVE ATTAINED."`

segments.voice: Start with this sit itself: if a little narrator shows up, I'm doing well at this, I'm calmer than yesterday, don't scold it. Just say it again with the I taken out: sitting, breathing, calm for now. Then let even those words fade, and stay with the breath.
No "I have attained." The one who has entered the stream doesn't think, I have entered it; Subhuti dwells in peace without that thought. Today's word.
Your line: without "I did." Subhuti's peace has no signature on it. Back tomorrow with section ten.

1127.title: A mind that rests on nothing (section 10)
1127.word: A mind that rests on nothing
1127.hook: a mind should arise that rests on nothing: the line said to have woken Huineng
1127.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen this line is studied closely and often recited, and the story of Huineng hearing the Diamond Sutra is told in the Platform Sutra, a text read in those schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no I have attained: Subhuti dwells in peace without the thought that he has. Your line: without I did.

A young man is selling firewood in a market town in southern China. He's poor, and the old account says he can't read. He delivers a load to a shop, and on the way out he hears a man reciting something. The words stop him where he stands. What is that? The Diamond Sutra, comes the answer. That's how the Platform Sutra, the book of this young man's life and teaching, tells it. His name is Huineng, and Chan and Zen remember him as a great ancestor. Later in the same account, one line of that sutra opens him all the way. It's today's.
screen: `A FIREWOOD SELLER.` → `A SUTRA HEARD IN PASSING.` → `HUINENG STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, a look back. The Buddha asks Subhuti: long ago, with the Buddha Dipankara, did the Tathagata receive any teaching? No, Subhuti says. Nothing was received. Second, adorning. Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-lands, make the worlds beautiful? No, because adorning is not adorning; that's why it's called adorning. It's the rhythm of the earlier sections. Third, the line. Therefore, the Buddha says, a bodhisattva should give rise to a pure mind like this: a mind that doesn't rest on sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts. A mind should arise that rests on nothing. Notice it doesn't say no mind should arise. The mind sees, hears, works. It just doesn't set up camp. A hand that catches a ball and lets it go is still a hand. Tradition says that later, when Huineng's teacher explained the sutra to him, it was at this line that he woke up completely. Fourth, the week. Giving without resting on anything. Not seen by marks. Even the raft. Nothing fixed. Four lines. No I have attained. Each was a place where the mind could have settled and made a home: the gift, the statue, the teaching, the prize, the credit. Each time, the sutra let it lift off again. Today's line names what was happening all week: the same mind, just not resting.
screen: `NOTHING RECEIVED FROM DIPANKARA.` · `ADORNING THAT ISN'T ADORNING.` · `A MIND THAT RESTS ON NOTHING.` · `A WEEK OF NOT SETTLING.` · then, large: `RESTING ON NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Let sounds come, a car, a fridge, your own breathing, and notice the mind land on one: that's a truck, that's too loud. Then let it lift, the way a bird lifts off a wire. You don't have to stop the landing; just catch one moment of lifting, and stay in the open space after it as long as it lasts.
A mind that rests on nothing. A mind that arises without resting on sights, sounds or thoughts: the line tradition says woke Huineng. Today's word.

chat.says: Does a mind that rests on nothing mean you should stop thinking?
options: No: the mind still sees, hears and works; it just doesn't set up camp anywhere.

It means the mind should hold tight to this one line and nothing else.
chat.meaning: The sutra says a mind should arise that rests on nothing. It doesn't say no mind should arise; the mind works, without clinging.
